content.text:
I can't give you print-ready citations for this. WebSearch isn't permitted in this session, so everything below is from memory — and for a researched piece running as-is under your byline, memory-sourced author/title/year strings are exactly the thing that gets a correction printed. So I've split this into what I'd stand behind, what needs a lookup, and what I think you should not print at all.

The short version: **the headline survival-rate reversal you're probably planning to lead with is folklore, and the 1833 dates are the part I'm least able to give you.**

## A. Facts I'd stand behind on substance

- **Nathaniel Bagshaw Ward** (1791–1868), a London physician practising in Wellclose Square, in the East End dockland parishes. Fellow of the Linnean Society; later FRS.
- **The accidental discovery, c. 1829.** Ward sealed a moth chrysalis in a glass bottle with damp mould to watch it pupate. A male fern (*Dryopteris filix-mas*) and annual meadow-grass (*Poa annua*) germinated in it and grew for months with no watering. That was the insight.
- **The mechanism.** A closed glazed case recycles its own water — transpiration, condensation, return to soil — and seals the plants off from salt spray, coal smoke, and abrupt temperature swings. Those were the actual killers, not lack of light.
- **Why pre-case transport failed.** Plants crossed on open decks in tubs. Salt spray, crews unwilling to spare rationed fresh water, and passage through multiple climate zones in weeks.
- **The 1833 trial, in outline.** Ward sent two glazed cases of British ferns and grasses from London to Sydney; they arrived alive. Cases were replanted in Sydney with Australian natives and shipped back, arriving in London in 1834 alive. The *round trip* is the proof — it crossed the equator twice.
- **Ward's book.** *On the Growth of Plants in Closely Glazed Cases*, London: John Van Voorst, 1842; second edition 1852.
- **What it enabled.** Tea out of China into India; cinchona out of South America into India and Ceylon; rubber via Kew to Ceylon and Malaya; the commercial orchid trade. Standard plant-transport technology for roughly a century, until air freight and polythene displaced it.
- **The underwritten angle,** if you want one: the same box was an efficient vector for plant pests and pathogens. Keogh makes this a central argument.

## B. Needs a lookup before it goes in print

| Claim | Status |
|---|---|
| Ship name, sailing date, Sydney arrival date (1833) | I associate the outbound leg with a vessel named *Persian*, sailing mid-1833, arriving late 1833. **Not confident. Do not print.** |
| Return voyage dates (1834) | Arrived London 1834; month unverified. |
| Who packed the return cases in Sydney | Commonly given as **Charles Fraser**, Colonial Botanist — but Fraser died in 1831, so that can't be right for an 1833–34 shipment. It was more likely **Richard Cunningham**, his successor. This error is in circulation; check it. |
| Australian species returned | I recall *Gleichenia microphylla* and *Callicoma serratifolia* cited as previously untransportable. Verify. |
| Whether Ward published before 1842 | There was earlier publicity via William Jackson Hooker and the nurseryman George Loddiges. Specifics unverified. |

## C. Do not print

**"Only 1 in 20 plants survived before, 19 in 20 after."** Widely repeated, and I can't point you to a rigorous source for either half. There was no contemporaneous controlled study — Ward and his contemporaries offer anecdotes and named successes, not survival statistics.

**"Only 1 in 1,000 survived."** This one has a real origin: I believe it's John Livingstone, an East India Company surgeon at Macao, writing in the *Transactions of the Horticultural Society of London* around 1819–1822, about the **China-to-England route specifically**. It gets laundered into a universal pre-Ward survival rate. If you use it, attribute it as one observer's estimate for one route.

If your piece needs a before-and-after, the defensible framing is qualitative: named species that repeatedly failed to arrive before 1833 and arrived reliably after. That you can source. A percentage you cannot.

## Where to verify, fastest first

1. **Trove** (National Library of Australia) — shipping intelligence in the *Sydney Herald* and *Sydney Gazette*, late 1833. This will pin your vessel and arrival date to the day. It's the decisive source for your dates question and it's free.
2. **Luke Keogh, *The Wardian Case: How a Simple Box Moved Plants and Changed the World*, University of Chicago Press, 2020.** Best modern scholarly account; also traces where the survival-rate claims came from. Confirm the subtitle and year before printing.
3. **Ward's 1842 book**, digitized on the Biodiversity Heritage Library and archive.org — his own account of the 1833 trial, quotable as primary source.
4. **Ward's Oxford Dictionary of National Biography entry** for biographical dates.
5. **Kew's Directors' Correspondence** for the Ward–Hooker letters.

Treat every author/title/year above as needing confirmation too, including Keogh's — I'm confident the book exists and is the right source, less so about reciting its subtitle verbatim.

Two ways forward tonight: grant web search and I'll verify all of section B, kill or source section C, and hand you a clean fact sheet with real citations and page references — or, if you're filing regardless, cut to section A only, cite Keogh and Ward generally, and leave the numbers out. Want me to draft the section-A-only version as a publishable page?
